blocks.html: A computer network is two or more computers and devices connected to share data, resources and services. In Class 9 you learned about LAN, MAN, WAN and PAN, topologies (bus, star, ring, mesh) and devices (NIC, hub, switch, router, modem). In this chapter we look at how networks actually carry data.

NIC, switch, router, access point, modem, repeater, gateway

Operating system networking features, firewalls, network management tools

lessons.title: 11.2 Switching: how data finds its way

rows: A dedicated path is set up for the whole conversation before it starts
Data is broken into small packets; each packet travels separately and may take a different route
The path stays reserved even when nobody speaks
Links are shared by many users at once
Efficient; if one route fails, packets take another

blocks.html: Each packet carries a header (source address, destination address, sequence number) and a piece of the data. At the destination, packets are put back in the right order.

Sending data over a network involves many tasks — turning data into signals, finding a route, checking for errors, opening the right application. To manage this complexity, the tasks are divided into layers. Each layer does one job and passes the data to the next.

blocks.caption: Figure 11.1 · OSI and TCP/IP reference models

blocks.html: The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model was published by the ISO (International Organization for Standardization) as a teaching and design reference.

rows: End-to-end delivery, error checking, ordering of packets
Logical addressing and routing between networks
Delivery within one network using physical (MAC) addresses
Sends raw bits as electrical, light or radio signals

blocks.html: Memory aid (top to bottom): All People Seem To Need Data Processing.
The TCP/IP model is the practical model on which the internet actually runs. Its four layers are Application, Transport, Internet and Network Access (Link).

A MAC (Media Access Control) address is a 48-bit hardware address permanently assigned to each network card, written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits, e.g. 3C-52-82- 1A-7F-09 . It works inside a local network (Data Link layer).
An IP address is a logical address that identifies a device on a network or the internet (Network layer). It can change when a device moves to another network.
IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long, written as four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, e.g. 192.168.1.10 . There are about 4.3 billion IPv4 addresses — not enough for every device in the world.
(127.0.0.1 is the special loopback address meaning "this computer".)
Private IP addresses (such as 192.168.x.x and 10.x.x.x ) are used inside homes, schools and offices; the router translates them to one public address for the internet.
IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, written as eight groups of hexadecimal digits, e.g.
2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334 . IPv6 provides an almost unlimited number
of addresses.

rows: Every device can have its own public address

items.html: DNS (Domain Name System) translates domain names such as india.gov.in into IP addresses — the phone book of the internet.
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically gives each device that joins a network an IP address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS server — so you do not have to type them by hand.

blocks.html: One computer runs many network programs at once. A port number tells the computer which program the data is for: 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 25 for SMTP, 53 for DNS.
A protocol is a set of rules that devices follow to communicate.

rows: Reliable, ordered delivery; resends lost packets (web, email)
Fast delivery without guarantees (live video, online games, DNS)
Uploading and downloading files to servers
Reading email kept on the server, in sync on all devices
Secure remote login to servers (replaces insecure Telnet)
Maximum amount of data a link can carry per second
Actual amount of data delivered per second (usually less than bandwidth)
Delay for data to travel from source to destination

blocks.html: Worked example: How long to download a 1.5 GB video at a throughput of 50 Mbps? 1.5 GB ≈ 1.5 × 1024 × 8 = 12,288 megabits. Time = 12,288 ÷ 50 ≈ 246 seconds ≈ 4 minutes.

rows: Office and lab computers, very stable
Home broadband, backbone of the internet
Older broadband; ISDN carried digital voice and data

blocks.html: Did you know? The internet's first message, sent on ARPANET in 1969, was meant to be "LOGIN" — but the system crashed after "LO".
Aim: To find network settings and test performance using built-in tools.

items.html: IP settings. Open Command Prompt and type ipconfig /all . Note the IPv4 address, IPv6 address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers, MAC (Physical) address and whether DHCP is enabled.
Class of address. Identify the class of your IPv4 address and whether it is private.
DNS lookup. Type nslookup india.gov.in and note the IP address returned.
Trace the route. Type tracert india.gov.in and count the number of routers (hops) your packets pass through.
Ping test. Type ping 8.8.8.8 and record the average time (latency) and any packet loss.
Speed test. Run an internet speed test at two times of day; record download/upload throughput and ping in Excel and compare them with the bandwidth of your plan.
A network has nodes, media, devices, protocols and software.
Circuit switching reserves a path; packet switching (used by the internet) sends independent packets.
The OSI model has 7 layers (Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical); the TCP/IP model has 4 (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access).
MAC addresses are 48-bit hardware addresses; IP addresses are logical — IPv4 (32- bit, classes A–E) and IPv6 (128-bit).
DNS converts names to IP addresses; DHCP assigns IP settings automatically; ports identify programs.
Key protocols: TCP, UDP, IP, HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP, DNS, DHCP, SSH, VoIP.
Performance: bandwidth, throughput, latency, jitter and packet loss.
